newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: ARA barges fully booked despite ending IPE duel.
newsitem.headline: ARA barges fully booked despite ending IPE duel.

text.p: Despite the imminent end to the IPE November gas oil duel, barges in the ARA region are still tied up, some by the delivery itself, others by growing gas oil demand into Switzerland, barge suppliers said on Thursday.

"There will be a lot of waiting time in ARA until the end of next week. Barges are still taking days when the (loading and discharge) points are only an hour's sailing apart," one barge supplier said.

The congestion comes towards the end of the record 865,100-tonne delivery of gas oil against expired Novemer IPE futures and the duel between two trading houses which are contracted to exchange the bulk of the volume.

The deliveries have been concentrated in Amsterdam and Antwerp, but, in their efforts to avoid these ports, charterers have caused queues in Rotterdam and Flushing. For some players still, there are simply no barges available.
"If you had 10 barges (available) today, they'd all be gone in an hour," said one supplier.
Rumours are also circulating that the delivery itself could continue into another week.
"We understand (deliveries against IPE November futures) have been prolonged to December 5 or 6," one barge supplier.
"They've given this tender another week," said another.
However, the dominant short in the gas oil delivery, AIC, said this was not the case.
"We have had no conversations with respect to extending (the delivery) by another week. To our knowledge, it will end on Saturday," said a trader at AIC.
Cargill, the dominant long, declined to comment.

Even without IPE-related deliveries, larger vessels could be kept busy heading up the Rhine after the reopening of a lock at Kembs, about 15 km downstream from Basle. The lock, the larger of two at Kembs, will reopen late on Saturday after a closure of around two months.

During that time, no barge longer than 95 metres could proceed into or out of Switzerland. Shipowners said the lock opening means that barges with up to 3,000 tonnes of product will be able to reach Basle and other upstream destinations. The larger deliveries will lead to a considerable saving in the freight rate per tonne.
"Yesterday, we closed many barges to Basle, with about 20,000-30,000 tonnes going in December," one barge supplier said.
